description: We are a team from Yahya Kemal High School Skopje and we will compete in the Nasa Space Apps Challenge
summary: Abandoned, But Not Forgotten tells the story of the machines NASA has left on the Moon and Mars to school-age space fans. Our presentation introduces the hardware in a timeline from Ranger 4 in 1962 to Ingenuity’s last flight in 2024. It then lets children meet the machines one by one: the Lunar Roving Vehicles, the Apollo landers, the laser mirrors that still work today, Opportunity, Perseverance and Ingenuity. Each machine card shows what it is, what it discovered, where it is now and whether it is still working or silent, with real numbers from NASA data. To make the science hands-on, we also built our own model rover. A joystick acts as mission control, an ultrasonic sensor acts as the rover’s eyes, and an Arduino sends live data to our C++ mission-control dashboard. When an obstacle comes too close, the rover plans its own detour with Pythagoras, the same idea NASA’s rovers use to drive themselves on Mars. Our project shows children that these machines are abandoned, but not forgotten, because their science still helps the next explorers.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Our project has two parts. The first is a 7-slide storytelling presentation for children. It starts with a Moon timeline and a Mars timeline, then introduces individual machines with “NASA DATA” panels (mass, size, distance driven, landing site) and a status label: “still working” or “silent”. Mission times on Mars are given in sols (1 sol = 24 h 39 min 35 s), and all units are SI.

The second part is our own rover model and simulation. An Arduino reads an analog joystick and an ultrasonic distance sensor and sends “x;y;distance” over USB every 50 ms. Our C++ program on the PC turns this into a live mission-control dashboard:

  • Speed follows the tilt of the joystick, from -50 to +50 m/s. Reversing gives a negative speed and lowers the distance travelled.
  • The heading is calculated with atan2 (the inverse tangent).
  • A radar bar shows how close the nearest obstacle is.
  • When an obstacle is closer than 10 cm, the rover plans a detour. It calculates the side step needed, the steering angle, and the length of each leg with Pythagoras, then shows how much farther it must drive than in a straight line. An event log records every change.

Benefits and impact:
Children learn about real NASA machines and the science they made possible, and then use the same ideas themselves: telemetry, vector maths and autonomous obstacle avoidance. The model is cheap (cardboard, Arduino, joystick, ultrasonic sensor), so any school can build it. We want to bring it to schools in Macedonia.

Tools and technologies:

  • Hardware: Arduino, analog joystick module, ultrasonic distance sensor, cardboard rover model, USB cable
  • Software: Arduino code, a C++ program using the Windows serial port API, and a colour console dashboard built with ANSI codes
  • Presentation: PowerPoint
  • Data: NASA data and mission pages (see the NASA Data section)

Creativity:
Instead of only telling the story of the hardware, we let children play the role of mission control. They drive a rover, watch it detect an obstacle, and see the maths it uses to get around it. This connects to why real Mars rovers must drive themselves: a signal takes several minutes to reach Mars.

Factors we considered:

  • Our audience is school-age children, so we used short texts, a timeline and status labels.
  • Every number is checked against NASA sources.
  • We used SI units and sols for Mars.
  • The model had to be low-cost.
  • The demo had to stay within the 7-slide limit.

Use of AI:
We used an AI assistant debugging our C++ code.
